p.src: The story tells how Tripitaka joyfully took leave of the prefect. As he rode along, he said to the Pilgrim, “Worthy disciple, the good accomplished here truly surpasses even the rescue of the children in the Kingdom of Bhikṣu. It is all owing to you.” Sha Monk said, “In the Kingdom of Bhikṣu we saved only one thousand one hundred and eleven children. How can that compare with this great torrential rain, which soaked the land and brought life to countless thousands upon thousands? I too have secretly admired our eldest brother’s powers, which reach through Heaven, and his compassionate grace, which covers the earth.” Bajie laughed. “Brother has shown kindness and done good, to be sure, but he dispenses benevolence to others while harboring malice within. Whenever Old Hog travels with him, he is forever tormenting me.” “Where have I tormented you?” asked the Pilgrim. “Enough, enough,” said Bajie. You are always arranging for me to be bound, arranging for me to be hung up, arranging for me to be boiled, or arranging for me to be steamed. Now that we have bestowed a blessing on countless people in Fengxian Prefecture, we ought to stay for half a year and let me enjoy a few hearty meals at leisure. Instead, you keep urging us onward.” Hearing this, the elder rebuked him. “You idiot! Why do you think of nothing but stuffing your mouth? Hurry on, and quarrel no more.” Bajie dared say no more. He pursed his lips, shouldered the baggage, and trudged along yawning as master and disciples took to the highway. Time flew like a shuttle, and deep autumn came round once more. They saw that:

p.src: After the four travelers had journeyed for a long while, the dim outline of city walls appeared once more. The elder raised his whip, pointed into the distance, and called, “Wukong, look! There is another city over there, but I wonder what place it may be?” “Neither you nor I have ever been here,” said the Pilgrim. “How could we know? Let us go up to it and ask someone.” Before he had finished speaking, an old man emerged from a grove. He held a bamboo staff, wore light garments, had a pair of coir sandals on his feet, and a flat sash around his waist. Tripitaka hastily tumbled from the saddle, went forward, and offered a greeting. Leaning on his staff, the old man returned the courtesy and asked, “From where have you come, venerable sir?” Tripitaka joined his palms and said, “This poor monk was sent from the Tang court in the Eastern Land to worship the Buddha at Thunderclap Monastery and seek the scriptures. Now that I have reached this honored region, I can see city walls in the distance but do not know what place this is, so I have especially come to ask your guidance, good patron.” Hearing this, the old man said, “You are indeed a monk of the Way. This humble region of ours is a subordinate prefecture of India, and the place is called Yuhua County. The lord of the city is a member of the Indian emperor’s clan and bears the title Prince of Yuhua. This prince is very virtuous: he reveres Buddhist and Daoist clergy and dearly cherishes the common people. If you go to see him, venerable master, he is certain to treat you with the greatest respect.” Tripitaka thanked him, and the old man went straight through the grove and disappeared.

p.src: Only then did Tripitaka turn and tell his disciples all that had passed. The three were delighted and helped their master onto his horse. “It is not far,” said Tripitaka. “There is no need to ride.” So all four walked to the streets by the city and looked about them. The houses in the suburbs belonged to merchants and tradespeople; the population was dense and business exceedingly prosperous. Judging by the people’s voices and appearance, the place differed in no way from China. Tripitaka instructed them, “Disciples, be careful and do not behave wantonly.” Bajie lowered his head, Sha Monk covered his face, and only Sun the Pilgrim walked openly, supporting his master. People on both sides crowded round to stare and cried in unison, “Here we have only seen eminent monks who subdue dragons and tame tigers. Never have we seen monks who subdue pigs and tame monkeys!” Unable to restrain himself, Bajie thrust out his snout and said, “Have you ever seen the monk who is king of the pig-subduers?” The people filling the street were so frightened that they stumbled over one another as they scattered to both sides. The Pilgrim laughed. “Idiot, put that snout away. Stop showing off and mind your step as we cross the bridge.” The idiot lowered his head and merely laughed. After crossing the drawbridge and entering the city gate, they saw taverns and singing houses along the main street, bustling and flourishing. It was indeed a great city of a divine land. p.src: Tripitaka rejoiced inwardly and thought, “People speak of the various foreign lands of the Western Regions, yet I have never before come to such a place as this. Looking closely at this scene, how does it differ from our Great Tang? This must truly be what is meant by the Land of Supreme Bliss.” He also heard people say that a picul of white rice cost four mace and a catty of sesame oil only eight cash. It was truly a land of abundant harvests.

p.src: After walking for a long while, they finally reached the residence of the Prince of Yuhua. On either side of the palace gate stood the Secretariat, the Judicial Hall, the Office of Provisions, and the Guest Lodge. Tripitaka said, “Disciples, this is the prince’s residence. Wait here while I go in to pay court to the prince, have our passport inspected, and then continue our journey.” Bajie said, “While Master goes inside, are we supposed to stand here in front of the government offices?” Tripitaka said, “Can you not see the three characters ‘Guest Lodge’ written over that doorway? !” All of you go and sit there. See whether they have fodder, and buy some to feed the horse. If the prince grants me a vegetarian meal when I see him, I shall come and summon you to enjoy it with me.” The Pilgrim said, “Go without worry, Master. Old Sun will see to everything.” Sha Monk carried the baggage into the lodge. The attendants in charge of the lodge saw how ugly they looked and dared neither question them nor tell them to leave. They could only let them sit there, and we shall speak no more of them for the moment.

p.src: Now we tell how the venerable master changed his robe and cap, took up the travel document, and went straight to the prince’s residence. An usher came forward at once to meet him and asked, “Where have you come from, venerable sir?” Tripitaka said, “I am a monk sent by the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to worship the Buddha at Great Thunderclap Monastery and seek the scriptures. Having now reached your honored territory, I wish to have my travel document endorsed and have therefore come to pay my respects to His Highness.” The usher immediately reported the matter to the prince. The prince was indeed worthy and enlightened; he immediately issued an order for the monk to enter. Tripitaka reached the foot of the hall and bowed. The prince at once invited him up into the hall and offered him a seat. Tripitaka presented the travel document. The prince examined it and saw the seals and signatures of the various kingdoms. He gladly stamped it with his precious seal, added his ornate signature, folded it up, and placed it on the table. He asked, “Reverend National Preceptor, how great a distance have you traveled through all the countries between your Great Tang and this place?” Tripitaka replied, “This poor monk has not kept account of the distance. But years ago, when the Bodhisattva Guanyin manifested herself before my sovereign, she left a verse saying that the West lay one hundred and eight thousand li away. On the road I have already passed through fourteen cycles of cold and heat.” The prince laughed. “Fourteen cycles of cold and heat make fourteen years. I suppose you suffered some delays along the way?” Tripitaka said, “It is a long story. Amid countless hibernating fiends and a thousand demons, I cannot say how much suffering we endured before reaching your honored region.” The prince was greatly delighted and immediately ordered the officer of provisions to prepare a vegetarian feast for his guest. Tripitaka said, “Your Highness, this poor monk has three humble disciples waiting outside. I dare not accept the meal, for I fear delaying our journey.” The prince ordered, “Officer in attendance, go quickly and invite the elder’s three disciples into the residence to share the meal.”

p.src: The court officials went outside with him to summon them, but all said, “We have not seen them. We have not seen them.” One of the attendants said, “There are three ugly-looking monks sitting in the guest lodge. They must be the ones.” The court officials went together to the lodge and asked its keeper, “Which of these are the eminent disciples of the Tang monk journeying to fetch the scriptures? Our lord has commanded that they be invited to partake of a vegetarian meal.” Bajie had been sitting there dozing, but when he heard the word “meal,” he could not help leaping to his feet and answering, “That is us! That is us!” At the sight of him, the court officials were scared out of their wits and cried, trembling, “A pig demon! A pig demon!” Hearing this, Pilgrim seized Bajie and said, “Brother, behave with some decorum. Do not act like a country bumpkin.” When the officials saw Pilgrim, they cried again, “A monkey spirit! A monkey spirit!” Monk Sha cupped his hands and said, “Gentlemen, do not be alarmed. All three of us are disciples of the Tang monk.” When the officials saw him, they cried yet again, “The Stove God! The Stove God!” Sun the Pilgrim then told Bajie to lead the horse and Monk Sha to shoulder the luggage, and they accompanied the officials into the residence of the Prince of Yuhua. The court official went in first to report their arrival.

p.src: When the prince raised his eyes and saw how hideous they were, even he felt afraid. Tripitaka pressed his palms together and said, “Your Highness, set your mind at ease. Though my unruly disciples are ugly in appearance, they are all good at heart.” Bajie saluted the throne and said, “This poor monk offers his greetings.” The prince grew still more frightened. Tripitaka said, “These unruly disciples of mine were all taken in from wild mountains and know nothing of courtly etiquette. I beg Your Highness to forgive them.” Suppressing his fear, the prince ordered the officer of provisions to take the monks to the Baosha Pavilion for their vegetarian meal. Tripitaka thanked him for his favor, took leave of the prince, and descended from the hall. When they had all reached the pavilion, he reproached Bajie: “You dolt! You have not the least notion of proper manners. It would have been better if you had kept your mouth shut altogether. Why did you have to be so coarse? A single utterance from you was enough to knock Mount Tai flat.” Pilgrim laughed and said, “Then it was just as well that I did not offer a greeting. It saved me some effort too.” Monk Sha said, “Even his salute was ill-timed. Before he had properly composed himself, he thrust out his snout and began bellowing.” Bajie said, “What a nuisance! What a nuisance! The other day Master told me it was polite to offer a greeting whenever I met someone. Today I offered one, and now you say that was wrong too. What am I supposed to do?” Tripitaka said, “I taught you to offer a greeting when you met people; I never taught you to pester a prince with such antics. As the common saying goes, ‘Things are divided into different ranks, and so are people.’ How could you fail to distinguish noble from base?” As they spoke, the officer of provisions arrived with his servants, set out the tables and chairs, and laid out the vegetarian meal. The master and disciples fell silent, and each began to eat.

p.src: Now the prince withdrew from the hall and entered the inner palace. There were three young princes within, and when they saw that his face had changed color, they asked, “Father, why do you look so frightened today?” The prince replied, “A little while ago, a monk sent from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to worship the Buddha and fetch scriptures came to exchange his travel rescript. He himself was a most distinguished-looking man. I invited him to partake of a vegetarian meal, and he said his disciples were waiting before the residence, so I immediately ordered that they be summoned. When they entered a short while later, they did not perform the grand obeisance before me, but merely offered a greeting, which already displeased me; but when I raised my head and looked, every one of them was as ugly as a fiend. I could not help being terrified, and that is why my face changed color.” Now those three young princes were unlike ordinary men: each was martial and eager to prove his strength. Rolling up their sleeves and brandishing their fists, they said, “Could they be demons come down from the mountains in human disguise? Let us fetch our weapons and go out to see.”

The prince replied, “A little while ago, a monk sent from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to worship the Buddha and fetch scriptures came to exchange his travel rescript. He himself was a most distinguished-looking man.
I invited him to partake of a vegetarian meal, and he said his disciples were waiting before the residence, so I immediately ordered that they be summoned.

but when I raised my head and looked, every one of them was as ugly as a fiend. I could not help being terrified, and that is why my face changed color.”

Now those three young princes were unlike ordinary men: each was martial and eager to prove his strength. Rolling up their sleeves and brandishing their fists, they said, “Could they be demons come down from the mountains in human disguise? Let us fetch our weapons and go out to see.”

p.src: Fine princes they were! The eldest took a staff as tall as his eyebrows, the second swung a nine-toothed rake, and the third wielded a black, oil-polished cudgel. Bold and high-spirited, they strode out of the royal residence and shouted, “Where are those monks fetching the scriptures?” The officer of provisions and the others present knelt and said, “Young Highnesses, they are taking their meal in the Baosha Pavilion.” Without pausing to distinguish right from wrong, the young princes burst inside and shouted, “Are you men or monsters? Speak at once, and we shall spare your lives.” Tripitaka was so frightened that the color drained from his face. Dropping his rice bowl, he bowed and said, “This poor monk has come from the Tang realm to fetch scriptures. I am a man, not a monster.” A young prince said, “You at least still look like a man, but those three ugly fellows are monsters beyond any doubt.” Bajie simply went on eating and paid them no heed. Monk Sha and Pilgrim rose slightly from their seats and said, “We are all men. Though our faces are ugly, our hearts are good; though our bodies are coarse, our natures are kind. But where have you three come from, that you boast and bluster so recklessly?” The officer of provisions and other officials nearby said, “These three are the young royal highnesses, sons of our king.” Bajie put down his bowl and said, “Young Highnesses, what are you all doing with those weapons? Do you mean to fight us?”

p.src: The second prince spread his stance, flourished the rake in both hands, and made ready to strike Bajie. Bajie chuckled and said, “That rake of yours is fit only to be the grandson of mine.” He lifted his robe, drew the rake from his waist, and gave it a shake, whereupon ten thousand shafts of golden light streamed forth. When he performed a few moves with it, a thousand streams of auspicious vapor arose. The sight frightened the prince so badly that his hands weakened and his sinews went numb, and he dared not flourish his weapon again. Seeing the eldest prince hopping about with a staff as tall as his eyebrows, Pilgrim took the Gold-Banded Cudgel from his ear and gave it a shake. It became as thick as a rice bowl and some twelve or thirteen feet long. He rammed it into the ground, driving it some three feet deep, and left it standing there. With a laugh he said, “I shall give you this cudgel.” Hearing this, the prince immediately threw down his own staff and went to take the cudgel. Gripping it with both hands, he pulled with all his strength, but could not move it the slightest fraction; he tried lifting it again and then shaking it, but it was as though it had taken root. The third prince gave rein to his reckless temper and came at them striking with his black, oil-polished cudgel. Monk Sha knocked it aside with one hand, drew forth his Demon-Subduing Treasure Staff, and twirled it. Brilliant light sprang forth, and rosy radiance shimmered all around. The officer of provisions and the other officials were so terrified that they stood there dazed and rigid, unable to utter a word. All three young princes bowed down together and said, “Divine masters! Divine masters! We ordinary mortals failed to recognize you. We earnestly beg you to display your arts for us, so that we may become your disciples and receive your instruction.” Pilgrim stepped forward, lightly lifted the cudgel, and said, “It is too cramped here for me to display my skill properly. Let me leap into the air and perform a full routine for you to watch.”

All three young princes bowed down together and said, “Divine masters! Divine masters! We ordinary mortals failed to recognize you. We earnestly beg you to display your arts for us, so that we may become your disciples and receive your instruction.”
Pilgrim stepped forward, lightly lifted the cudgel, and said, “It is too cramped here for me to display my skill properly.
Let me leap into the air and perform a full routine for you to watch.”

p.src: Our great sage gave a whistle, flipped into a somersault, and rose into the air upon five-colored auspicious clouds, some three hundred paces above the ground. He flourished his gold-banded staff in the forms called “Scattered Blossoms Crown the Head” and “Yellow Dragon Turns Its Body,” sweeping it up and down and wheeling it left and right; at first, man and staff together seemed like flowers embroidered upon brocade. later the man vanished from sight, and only a sky full of rolling staff-shadows remained. Bajie cheered from below and, unable to keep still himself, shouted, “Let old Pig go up and have some fun too!” That fine idiot mounted a gust of wind and rose into the air. He set his rake flying—three strokes above and four below, five to the left and six to the right, seven before and eight behind—displaying every skill he possessed amid the ceaseless roar of wind. Just as the display reached its height, Sha the Monk said to the elder, “Master, let old Sha go and exercise his skills as well.” That worthy monk sprang upward with both feet, whirled his staff, and rose into the air, where a keen aura gathered in mist and golden light shimmered faintly. With both hands he worked the demon-subduing staff through “Cinnabar Phoenix Faces the Sun” and “Hungry Tiger Pounces on Its Prey,” pressing hard, parrying softly, wheeling swiftly, and darting nimbly. The three brothers displayed their divine powers high in the air, all showing their might and martial splendor together. Truly it was a sight of which one might say:

p.src: The three young princes hurried back to the palace and reported to the old king: “Father, this is cause for boundless joy! Today we have gained an extraordinary opportunity. Did you see the display in midair just now?” The old king replied, “I saw rosy clouds in the sky and at once burned incense and bowed in the palace courtyard with your mother and the others, but I did not know what immortals had descended and gathered here.” The princes said, “They were no immortals from elsewhere, but the three ugly disciples of that scripture-seeking monk. One wields a gold-banded iron staff, another a nine-pronged muckrake, and the third a precious demon-subduing staff. Compared with theirs, our three weapons are utterly worthless. We asked them to demonstrate a round, and they said, ‘The ground is too cramped for us to move freely. Let us rise into the air and show you a round there.’ Then each mounted a cloud, until the whole sky shimmered with auspicious clouds and swirled with a blessed aura. They have only just descended and are all seated in the Baosha Pavilion. We are overjoyed and wish to take them as our masters, learn their arts, and protect our realm. This would truly be an achievement beyond measure. What does Father think?” Hearing this, the old king believed them and gladly consented to their wish.

p.src: At once the father and his three sons went on foot to the Baosha Pavilion, without carriage or canopy. The four pilgrims had packed their luggage and were about to enter the residence to offer thanks for the meal and take leave of the king when they happened to see the King of Yuhua and his sons mounting the pavilion and prostrating themselves. The elder, flustered, straightened himself and fell to the ground to return their bow, while Wukong and the others slipped aside with faint, chilly smiles. When all had finished bowing, the pilgrims were invited into the residence and seated in the main hall. The four entered gladly. The old king rose and said, “Reverend Master from the Tang, I have a favor to ask. I wonder whether your three accomplished disciples might consent?” Tripitaka replied, “Whatever Your Majesty commands, my humble disciples will not dare disobey.” The old king said, “When I first met you gentlemen, I took you merely for wandering monks who had come from the distant Tang. Being a mortal of fleshly eyes, I treated you with much disrespect. Only after seeing Master Sun, Master Zhu, and Master Sha perform in the air did I realize that you are immortals and buddhas. My three unworthy sons have loved the martial arts all their lives. They now sincerely wish to become your disciples and learn some martial skill. I earnestly beg you, reverend masters, to open your hearts as broad as heaven and earth, launch the universal vessel of compassion, and instruct my sons. I shall surely offer the wealth of the entire city in gratitude.” Hearing this, Wukong could not help laughing aloud. “Your Highness, you truly do not understand how things are done. We who have left the household could wish for nothing better than to pass our teaching on to a few disciples. Since your noble sons are minded to follow the good, you must never speak of the slightest payment. Treat us only with friendship and goodwill; that affection will be more than enough.”

p.src: When the princes heard this, each bowed again and again with his head to the ground. The three stepped forward, bowed deeply, and sincerely begged to be instructed. Wukong asked, “What sort of martial art do you three wish to learn?” The princes replied, “The one who wishes to wield a cudgel will learn the cudgel; the one accustomed to the rake will learn the rake; and the one who favors the staff will learn the staff.” Wukong laughed. “Teaching you would be easy enough, but you lack the strength to wield our weapons. I fear your learning would remain imperfect, like one who tries to paint a tiger but ends by producing something resembling a dog. The ancients said, ‘If instruction is not strict, the fault lies in the teacher’s indolence; if learning bears no fruit, the blame lies with the pupil.’ Since you are sincere, go and burn incense and bow to Heaven and Earth. I shall first impart some divine strength to you, and only then can I teach you the martial arts.”

p.src: When the three young princes heard this, their hearts filled with joy. They personally carried in an incense table, washed their hands, lit incense, and bowed in worship toward Heaven. When they had finished bowing, they asked their masters to impart the art to them. Wukong turned around, bowed to the Tang Monk, and said, “Revered Master, I beg you to pardon your disciple’s offense. Ever since your great benevolence delivered me from the Mountain of Two Frontiers and received me into the Buddhist order, I have journeyed westward with you. Though I have never adequately repaid your kindness, I have crossed rivers and climbed mountains, sparing no effort. Now that we have reached this land of the Buddha, we have had the good fortune to meet the worthy king’s three sons, who have bowed to us as disciples and wish to learn martial arts. Since they are our disciples, they are therefore your grand-disciples. I respectfully report this to you so that we may properly instruct them.” Tripitaka was exceedingly pleased. Seeing Wukong bow, Bajie and Sha Monk also turned and kowtowed to Tripitaka, saying, “Master, we are dull-witted and clumsy-tongued, and do not know how to speak properly. We beg you to take the honored seat of the Dharma and let each of us take a disciple for amusement; it will also give us something by which to remember our journey to the Western Heaven.” Tripitaka gladly consented to everything.

p.src: Wukong then had a Dipper diagram drawn in a quiet chamber behind the gauze pavilion for the three princes. He told all three to lie face down within it, close their eyes, and calm their spirits. He secretly recited the true formula and chanted an incantation, blowing immortal breath into the hearts and bellies of the three and restoring their primal spirits to their native abodes. He imparted the secret formula to them, bestowed immense strength upon each, and advanced the tempering of their inner power; it was like a method of remaking their very bodies and bones. Only after the energy had circulated through the full zi-wu circuit did the three young princes awaken. They all scrambled to their feet, wiped their faces, and stood brimming with vigor, every one of them strong in bone and sinew: the eldest prince could now wield the gold-banded cudgel, the second could swing the nine-pronged rake, and the third could raise the demon-quelling staff.

p.src: The old king was overjoyed at the sight. He prepared another vegetarian banquet to express his gratitude to the master and his three disciples. Right there before the feast, each master began teaching his own pupil: the one learning the cudgel practiced the cudgel, the one learning the rake practiced the rake, and the one learning the staff practiced the staff. Though they managed several turns and displayed a number of techniques, they were mortals after all and had to exert themselves. After one routine they were already panting and could not endure for long. For those weapons could all change their form; in advance and retreat, attack and flourish, they shrank and grew at will, possessing a natural and wondrous efficacy. How could mere mortals master them in so short a time? That day the banquet came to an end.

p.src: The next day, the three princes came again to offer thanks, saying, “Through the divine masters’ favor we have been endowed with strength. Though we can now swing our masters’ weapons, changing from one movement to another remains difficult. We wish to order smiths to copy the divine masters’ weapons, reducing their weight and forging others of the same shape. We do not know whether our masters will permit it.” Bajie said, “Good, good, good! That makes perfect sense. For one thing, you cannot properly wield our weapons; for another, we need them to protect the Dharma and subdue demons. You certainly ought to have new ones made.” The princes immediately summoned blacksmiths and purchased ten thousand jin of iron and steel. They erected a workshop in the front courtyard of the royal residence, set up furnaces, and began forging. On the first day, they refined and tempered the iron and steel. The next day, they asked Wukong and his two companions to take out the gold-banded cudgel, the nine-pronged rake, and the demon-quelling staff and place them in the covered workshop so the smiths could copy their forms. Thus the work continued without ceasing, day or night.
